title: Sorry, haters. Ferrari’s first EV is doing just fine
teaser: Despite initial hate, Ferrari's polarizing debut EV, the Luce, hit its sales target fast, showing strong demand from China.
summary: Against initial critical backlash and predictions of failure, Ferrari's first electric vehicle (EV), the Luce, has exceeded expectations. Initially criticized for its polarizing design, the car was largely designed by Jony Ive/LoveFrom. Despite early setbacks, sales reports indicate that Ferrari reached its projected target for the Luce quickly. This success is reportedly fueled by strong demand from China and wealthy buyers in tech hubs like Silicon Valley. Priced around €555,000, the company plans to sell approximately 2,500 units by 2030, marking a significant pivot into the EV market.
author: Tim De Chant
content: Sometimes the crowd isn't so wise. When Ferrari revealed the Luce - its first EV - to the public in May, the internet reacted. And not in a positive way. Critics compared the wedge-shaped Luce with a Nissan Leaf and said Chinese EVs would outperform it while undercutting it on price. Even former Ferrari chair Luca Cordero di Montezemolo was among the haters. Ferrari's stock dropped 8% the day after the reveal. Their conclusion: the Luce would be a dud. It turns out, the armchair auto executives were wrong about the five-seater that was largely designed by Jony Ive and his firm, LoveFrom. Ferrari hit this year's sales target for the Luce in just two months, according to a report by the Financial Times. The automaker was hoping to sell just under 500 of the €555,000 EVs ($630,000), and based on previous reports , it sounds like at least 20% will make their way to China. That's not surprising, given that the Luce seems tailor-made for the Chinese market , which favors fast, sleek four-door EVs. TechCrunch has reached out to Ferrari to confirm the figures, and we'll update this article if we receive a reply. Much of the internet's hate was directed at the Luce's styling, which hewed to some Ferrari norms while throwing others out the window. Appearance is subjective, and I've seen enough cars in my day to know that some designs don't translate well on screen. Maybe seeing one in person tipped buyers into placing an order. What's more, Ferrari has an enthusiastic and price-insensitive customer base. The company sold more than 13,000 cars last year, which is a lot for an automaker that specializes in six-figure vehicles. Ferrari buyers tend to own several models, so it's also not difficult to imagine 500 of them wanting a practical vehicle that's also a Ferrari. Is the Luce worth the price of admission? Early reviews suggest that it drives like a Ferrari should. Plus, it has the prancing horse on the hood. That appears to be all Ferrari needs to succeed.

title: The US government just banned Roombas
teaser: The new robot ban is far broader than humanoids: it threatens vacuum cleaners and delivery bots if they aren't built using US components.
summary: The FCC is banning new imports of 'advanced robotic devices,' citing national security risks linked primarily to foreign (especially Chinese) manufacturing. While headlines focused on humanoid robots, the ban's definition is much broader: it covers any ground-traveling, wireless robot weighing over 4.4 pounds—encompassing vacuum cleaners and delivery bots alike. The policy effectively impacts most roborobotic companies because top players are largely China-based. Companies seeking waivers must commit to local US manufacturing processes and design. Crucially, the FCC confirmed that existing devices already in use, such as current Roombas or routers, remain unaffected by the ban.
author: Sean Hollister
content: When the Trump administration announced yesterday that it was banning "advanced robotic devices" from entering the United States , the headlines were all about humanoids . But spying doesn't require legs - and neither does the FCC's robot ban. The robot ban will sweep up robot vacuum cleaners too , FCC media relations director Katie Gorscak confirms to The Verge. It's not coming for your existing Roomba, and companies can keep importing and selling already approved ones. But the government claims that future foreign robots pose a national security risk, and even robovac companies are suddenly being asked to commit to US manufacturing. While the government did include "humanoid robots" and "quadrupeds" among the bots it wants to ban, the ban is far broader than that. It covers almost any new software-controlled robot that travels over the ground, weighs more than 4.4 pounds (including any dock), can perceive its environment, and has wireless connectivity. By that definition, the FCC is banning future robot lawnmowers, sidewalk delivery robots, and the robots that crate around packages at your local Amazon warehouse. How the government defines the "advanced robotic devices" that will be banned from import. Image: FCC It was already clear from the government's ban announcement that it was thinking about robot vacuums. In the National Security Determination that the FCC is using to justify the ban, the government explicitly calls out my reporting on the incredibly poor security that let one man access 7,000 DJI robovacs around the world . But like the consumer router ban , the FCC isn't actually targeting companies with poor security. It's targeting basically every robovac company, regardless of their security practices - because basically every robovac is manufactured outside the US. The FCC is literally demonizing human and dog-shaped robots in this image tweeted by chair Brendan Carr. But that's the tip of the iceberg. Image: FCC Even before the US-based maker of the Roomba went bankrupt , its robots were built by a Chinese company. Just like Apple and Google and most every other gadget brand, these things are not produced domestically. Today, the vast majority of robot vacuums are designed by Chinese companies, too - all of the top five, including Roborock, Ecovacs, Dreame, Xiaomi, and Narwal, are Chinese entities. Even Dyson is turning to Chinese manufacturers . Following bankruptcy, the Roomba brand is now owned by its former China-based contract manufacturer Picea . "There are very few non-Chinese brands these days and their share is so small that it's difficult to track," IDC analyst Jitesh Ubrani tells The Verge . Even Matic, our top robovac pick that's assembled in California, may have to apply for a waiver for new models. It doesn't yet source 65 percent of components from the United States, co-founder and CEO Mehul Nariyawala tells The Verge . Because yes, even US companies need to swear their robots are made in the US to get the government's waiver. Meanwhile, foreign companies will need to swear they're investing in US manufacturing - or lie, like that DJI front company I wrote about . If Trump and Carr were focused on actually protecting US citizens from the incredibly worrying security practices of smart home companies, I might argue that the FCC shouldn't exempt cleaning robots, as they can spy just as effectively as a humanoid. The DJI Romo robovac was a chilling example, letting someone on the other side of the planet map out my colleague Thomas Ricker's home , but it gets much worse - read about the robot lawnmower that ran me over to hear how. But again, the government isn't asking these companies any questions about security - not one - to get the waiver that lets them through. The FCC only wants to know where they're designed and made and assembled and tested and influenced, and get a specific commitment to start manufacturing them in the US instead. Even then, it appears the FCC will simply preference US companies without any new commitments to security or US manufacturing, like it did when it almost immediately let Netgear off the hook - even though Netgear's routers were among those targeted in the Volt Typhoon incident that helped justify the router ban to begin with. Four unnamed sources told Reuters that "the FCC is expected to exempt many non-Chinese suppliers from the restrictions." The government isn't de facto banning every type of robot made outside the US without its special waiver. It already has exceptions for self-driving cars and trains, unmanned aircraft and underwater vehicles, surgical robots, wheelchairs, and fixed robot arms for industrial and medical use. But most robots now have an uncertain future in the United States. It's also worth repeating that the FCC is not coming for your existing robots, just like it isn't coming for your existing routers or drones. But it's also worth repeating that if these gadgets truly pose a national security risk, it's kind of silly to do nothing about the ones we've already purchased. title: Big vacuum is watching as robo-cleaners put humans behind the wheel
teaser: Robot maid services are here, but beware: they require joint human/AI control and record *all* private activity for AI training.
summary: San Francisco residents can hire specialized cleaning robots from Tau Robotics for $30/hour. Though showcasing advanced capabilities via models like 'Chelsea' and 'Elon,' the service is not fully autonomous; it requires joint control between an AI policy and a human operator who guides the tasks, much like automated driving today. While Tau claims robust technology (using parts from Unitree), privacy remains a major concern. Robots capture full video of every person in the home for training their AI models, which are stored indefinitely.
content: offbeat Big vacuum is watching as robo-cleaners put humans behind the wheel Like a Waymo mated with a Roomba The dream of having a mechanical maid to clean your home is real ... sort of. San Francisco residents can now hire a robot cleaner for just $30 an hour, but there's a catch. The robots are at least partially controlled by humans who are watching your home remotely. Tau Robotics cofounder and CEO Alexander Koch announced in a post on X Tuesday that his company was launching the waitlist for its invite-only cleaning services on Tau's website . Bereft of details like the specifics of the robot's capabilities, Tau's website is instead largely devoted to videos of the diminutive, router-headed, frog-eyed robot doing stuff. It's shown in various videos and still shots hopping out of a minivan and grabbing its work bag, wiping down the inside of a refrigerator, cleaning surfaces, vacuuming, and emptying trash cans with its pincer-like hands. The site also presents three featured house-cleaning robots for San Francisco: "Chelsea," which specializes in cleaning kitchens and bathrooms; "Elon," which Tau says learns where household items belong after a few recurring visits and returns them there; and "Tony," a deep-cleaning specialist. Koch claimed on X that none of the videos of the robot are sped up to make it look more natural, giving it a weirdly human way of moving that suggests Tau has developed a pretty robust robot - if the company is the one that actually designed it. That doesn't appear to be the case, however. Koch told us that the robot's cameras, claws, and onboard compute system were designed in house, but the rest of the hardware comes from Chinese robot maker Unitree. Hopefully Tau has enough spares lying around since the Trump administration just banned imports of foreign robots. Peek-a-boo: Tau operators see you There's also a big catch to this entire thing, as Koch notes in his post: It ain't exactly autonomous. "Each humanoid is jointly controlled by a human operator and AI," the Tau CEO said. An AI policy is always controlling the robot's motors, Koch explained in a LinkedIn chat, but there's always a human involved, too. "A human operator is always guiding that [AI] policy, sometimes directly and sometimes through higher-level instructions," Koch said. "The balance varies by task." The Tau CEO went on to tell us that he sees the project as "conceptually similar to autonomous driving," meaning that human operators are fully behind the wheel for now, and over time will only be there for safety before eventually being phased out entirely. As explained further in the company's service privacy policy , each robot is controlled in real time by a human operator during cleaning visits, although Tau says the robots are jointly controlled by AI and a human operator. Some operators are Tau employees and some are placed through a staffing agency, but all of them are working on-site at Tau's facility and have been background checked and trained by Tau, the company claims. "We plan to enable remote supervision from other locations in the future," Koch told us. That said, the robots are still capturing video to train Tau's AI cleaning models that the company said it hopes "will eventually do the job without a human operator." That video is stored indefinitely unless customers request it be deleted. Operators, support staff, engineers, and third-party service providers all have access to those videos even if Tau doesn't sell them or share anything for advertising purposes, and the company said recordings will include full video of every person in the home as well. Be sure to put some pants on before the thing visits, in other words. If you're still keen to let a human-operated robomaid into your house, you'd better get in line: Koch told us that each cleaning session is just one hour and so far "several hundred people" have signed up to be granted a spot. ®

title: NOAA ditches weather-predicting supercomputers for Google Cloud
teaser: NOAA is abandoning its own weather-predicting supercomputers for Google Cloud, marking a major shift in how critical national forecasts are generated.
summary: The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) plans to migrate its core weather forecasting system from proprietary supercomputers to Google Cloud by December 2027. Previously run on HPE Cray machines (like Dogwood and Cactus), this move transitions critical operations to the commercial cloud, making model forecasting more nimble. Experts note that while this development reduces the reliance on government-funded in-house HPC systems, it allows NOAA flexibility—such as scaling compute power for tropical storm season. The agency will leverage Google Cloud H4D VMs (built on AMD Epyc processors) and integrate DeepMind's AI tools to build an AI Global Forecast System, promising highly accurate forecasts using fewer computer cycles and generating results in minutes rather than hours.
content: HPC NOAA ditches weather-predicting supercomputers for Google Cloud Government agency will use Google Cloud H4D VMs to replace HPE Cray machines Uncle Sam will no longer be hosting his own supercomputers to predict the weather. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has picked Google Cloud to provide the infrastructure for its weather forecasting operations. In an announcement, NOAA boasted that it will be the first national weather prediction center to run on the commercial cloud, though the UK's Met Office is also in the process of moving its own weather prediction system to Microsoft Azure in a hybrid setup. Weather operations are typically run on in-house or government-funded supercomputer systems , which helps drive the HPC (high performance computing) market . General Dynamics held the previous contract for managing NOAA's weather predicting machines, which most recently were HPE Cray supercomputers running in data centers in Virginia and Arizona. Those machines - Dogwood and Cactus - could crank almost 14 PFlops of weather-predicting prognosis. The plan is to move NOAA's Weather and Climate Operational Supercomputing System, run by the National Weather Service (NWS) division, over to the cloud by December 2027, along with the software that generates NWS weather data for analysis. Don't say global warming The agency is hoping that the cloud will make model forecasting more nimble, resulting in earlier predictions and better warnings for all the extreme weather events that seem to keep occurring these days. It was the in-house systems that were holding things back, evidently. "Cloud-based high-performance computing will accelerate the transition of research into operations by eliminating traditional bottlenecks of on-premise systems," said NOAA Administrator Neil Jacobs in a statement . Jacobs noted that the cloud's flexibility for providing large amounts of compute is advantageous: the agency can ramp up cycles during tropical storm season, then wind them down during calmer periods. Under the contract, NOAA can also avail itself of Google's DeepMind set of AI tools to help build out its first AI-driven weather forecasting system, the AI Global Forecast System, which promises to offer accurate weather forecasts using 99.7% fewer computer cycles and take minutes, rather than hours, to produce a forecast. NWS has already been upgrading the software downstream from GFS and GEFS to also work in the cloud. In March, it awarded contracts to Accenture and Booz Allen Hamilton to oversee the development of cloud-based software (HIVE and CIRRUS) for the field offices to analyze data and push out alerts, replacing the in-house software doing these tasks currently. For the job, Google plans to use Google Cloud H4D VMs , built on AMD Epyc processors. Google labels these instances as "virtual machines" because they run under a hypervisor that integrates Google's networking and orchestration tools. As a result, they can be synchronized to run large jobs the same way supercomputers do. According to Google, customers can access H4Ds for as low as 3 cents per core-hour without long-term commitments. For supercomputing jobs, they can also use Cluster Toolkit to deploy clusters and Cluster Director to maintain them. Google Cloud's Batch can handle the queuing, scheduling, and resource provisioning. ®

title: Thinking Machines co-founder Lilian Weng left the company citing health reasons, then joined OpenAI
teaser: Lilian Weng stepped down from Thinking Machines citing health issues, but immediately rejoining OpenAI to spearhead research on 'recursive self-improvement.'
summary: Lilian Weng, co-founder of Thinking Machines, announced her departure due to health concerns, stating the startup's high workload was unsustainable. Despite this declaration, she has rapidly rejoined OpenAI, where she previously served as VP of AI Safety Research. At OpenAI, Weng will lead a top-level team accelerating internal research focused on 'recursive self-improvement'—a key concept in advanced AI allowing systems to iteratively enhance their own power. This high-profile move is notable amid the intense competition for talent among major AI labs.
author: Amanda Silberling
content: Lilian Weng, co-founder of Thinking Machines , announced this week that she would step down from her role, citing health issues. "I don't feel I'm able to continue at the pace a startup requires," she wrote in an internal Slack message, which she also shared on X. "After thinking about it for several months, I ultimately have to admit that the amount of consistent stress and workload have pushed me beyond what my health can sustain physically." On Wednesday, OpenAI told TechCrunch that Weng would be rejoining the company, where she previously served as the VP of AI Safety Research. According to a company spokesperson, Weng will lead a top-level team focused on accelerating OpenAI's internal research. This team will support cross-research work on recursive self-improvement, a process that would allow an AI system to iterate on itself to become more powerful. This move could be read as contradictory to Weng's statements about the impact of working at a fast-paced startup on her health - however, she likely won't face as much direct pressure while working at a company where she isn't a co-founder. Still, in a time of fierce competition for talent among AI labs, this high-profile departure is notable. Thinking Machines co-founder and former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati replied to Weng's X post earlier this week and expressed support for her decision to focus on her health. It is unclear if Murati was aware that Weng would rejoin OpenAI. "We'll miss you, it's been wonderful building Thinky together. I'm glad that you're putting your health first. Thank you for everything," Murati wrote in response to Weng's post.

title: AI's top startups are barely publishing their research
teaser: A study found that over half of AI startups have barely published research, raising concerns about validation and reproducibility in the booming sector.
summary: Despite making bold promises, major AI companies struggle with scientific documentation. A new analysis of 317 'AI unicorns' (private firms valued at over $1B) from 1998-2025 revealed that more than half have never been a leading author on a qualifying paper. This lack of publishing makes it difficult to verify and reproduce AI claims, prompting questions about scientific rigor. Experts suggest this reflects corporate incentives—where the goal is advancing money rather than science—or the need for faster timelines, leading companies to embrace 'blogification' over academic journals. The top 5% of firms account for over 90% of citations, with OpenAI responsible for nearly 40%. While China-based firms are noted for open-source models, the overall industry challenge remains: how to ensure safety and accountability without proper documentation.
author: YeGoblynQueenne
content: Today's biggest artificial intelligence (AI) startups make no shortage of bold promises. Their technologies, some boast, will revolutionize software development, drug discovery, and scientific research. Yet a new preprint posted on 16 July on bioRxiv suggests many of these firms barely participate in one of science's most fundamental practices: publicly documenting discoveries in scientific literature so other researchers can evaluate and build on them. More than half of AI unicorns-private companies valued at more than $1 billion-have never played a leading role in publishing a scientific paper or preprint, according to the new analysis. Collectively, they accounted for just one in every 1000 AI papers published in 2025 . "For a field that is supposedly reshaping science and is so advanced in terms of scientific potential, not having any scientific documentation seems like a very weird paradox," says paper co-author John Ioannidis, a metascientist at Stanford University. "How can you judge that what they say is real, validated, and reproducible?" The scarcity of publications, others say, also makes it harder to assess AI's social impacts, including energy use and safety. But University of Alberta AI ethicist Mohamed Abdalla says the findings reflect the incentives facing commercial AI developers, rather than solely a failure to uphold scientific norms. "It's not the company's job to advance science, right?" he says. "The company's job is to advance money." Ioannidis has long studied how unicorns, particularly in biotech, engage with the scientific literature. (In 2015, he was the first to publicly scrutinize the lack of peer-reviewed studies produced by Theranos , the blood testing startup that proved to be based on fraudulent data.) He wondered whether AI unicorns would show similar patterns. To find out, he and his team first identified all 317 unicorn AI companies that have existed from 1998 to 2025. Then, they searched for publications affiliated with these startups-including journal articles, conference papers, reviews, and preprints. They selected those where a company researcher played a leading role as a first or last author, indicating the startup had made a substantial contribution to the work. The final data set included 2077 final publications, comprising 1389 peer-reviewed papers and 688 preprints. More than half of the startups had never produced a single qualifying paper, the analysis revealed. Scientific influence proved even more concentrated, with the top 5% of firms accounting for greater than 90% of all citations. OpenAI alone was responsible for nearly 40% of all citations in the data set, followed by the Chinese computer vision company Megvii and the platform Hugging Face. And even at the most prolific companies, much of the output came from the same small group of repeat authors. For example, despite OpenAI employing roughly 4500 people, only eight researchers had authored five or more qualifying papers. The findings are unsurprising to some AI researchers given how the industry is structured. For example, unlike the pharmaceutical industry, where published discoveries can be protected by patents, AI companies have learned they often gain little from publicly disclosing technical advances, says Nur Ahmed, an AI researcher at the University of Arkansas. Google's landmark 2017 paper on the transformer-the architecture that underpins today's large language models-has become a classic cautionary example, Abdalla adds. Although Google patented aspects of the technology, "I don't think anybody's paying Google for that," he says. Startups also operate on much faster timelines than academia, where peer review can lumber on for months or even years. That's why many AI companies have embraced what Avijit Ghosh, an AI policy researcher at Hugging Face, calls the "blogification" of research: announcing new models and releasing code or data sets through blog posts and technical reports rather than scientific journals. The new analysis didn't track those outputs, he points out. For Ghosh, the debate shouldn't center on publishing in journals versus blogs. What matters is whether companies are releasing enough code, data sets, or model weights (the numbers that determine how a model interprets and responds to a prompt) for others to independently verify and build on their work, he says. The preprint also found that firms based in China consistently published more papers than their counterparts based in the United States. Whereas leading U.S. frontier labs have increasingly kept the details of their most capable models secret or "closed sourced," leading Chinese companies have embraced "open-source" models. Moonshot AI, one of the Chinese startups included in the study, recently unveiled Kimi K3-one of the strongest open models to date-and publicly released its model weights through Hugging Face today. But whether models are open or closed, the rapid pace toward increasingly powerful generalist AI worries Emma Pierson, a computer scientist at the University of California, Berkeley. She argues AI research-whether published freely or kept secret-risks accelerating models that pose serious societal and safety concerns, including supercharging cyberattacks . "If we were racing forward on cancer-curing AI, I would be like, 'Fantastic, full steam ahead,'" she says. "But that's not what we're racing toward, right?" author: Maria Deutscher
content: OpenAI Group PBC today launched a program that will give 100,000 researchers free access to ChatGPT's advanced features. ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is part of a $250 million OpenAI initiative designed to support scientific projects. The initiative also includes several other programs. Last May, OpenAI made $50 million worth of artificial intelligence resources available to a group of universities. This month, it announced plans to support multiple U.S. Energy Department research projects. Scientists can apply to ChatGPT for Academic Researchers via a form on OpenAI's website. Initially, the program will be open to 10,000 users at a limited number of universities. OpenAI plans to onboard 90,000 more researchers over time. According to the company, participants will receive access to a version of ChatGPT with "higher usage limits and larger context windows." OpenAI also plans to provide an "expanded" edition of the chatbot service's deep research feature. The capability, which debuted last February, can collect information from hundreds of websites to answer user questions. Researchers can alternatively configure it to focus on specific sources such as scientific journals. A scientist who is invited to OpenAI's new program can onboard four colleagues from the same academic institution. Those researchers receive access to the same set of features at no charge. According to OpenAI, the version of ChatGPT offered through the program ships with its latest large language models. The includes the company's flagship GPT-5.6 Sol algorithm. In particular, scientists will receive access to a version of the LLM called GPT-5.6 Sol Pro that is optimized for difficult queries and long-running tasks. The program also includes Codex and ChatGPT Work. The latter tool, the latest addition to OpenAI's lineup of productivity features, can automate sequences of relatively complex tasks. For example, a user could ask ChatGPT Work to summarize a set of customer support requests, turn the key findings into a graph and then embed the graph in a slide. The program also includes certain supporting resources. OpenAI will provide training on how to apply ChatGPT to complex research tasks. title: Back of the NetApp: Latest exec signing scores $34M compensation package
teaser: NetApp’s exec salaries hit record highs, with one chief scoring $34.27M—fueled by surging demand for AI infrastructure.
summary: NetApp’s recent executive pay package, notably Chief Product Officer Syam Nair’s $34.27 million compensation for fiscal 2026, underscores the high costs of talent at major tech firms. This spending is supported by robust company performance: NetApp's American storage unit grew revenue 5.4% to $6.93 billion, and overall operating income increased 25% to $1.67 billion. The company has logged over 1,100 AI and data preparation deals, driving its share price up roughly 60% year-to-date. Even CEO George Kurian received significant compensation ($22.16 million). Investor support remains strong, highlighted by the 'say-on-pay' vote receiving 94% approval at the last annual meeting.
content: Storage Back of the NetApp: Latest exec signing scores $34M compensation package Product chief shoots straight to the top of the pay league, out-earning CEO in fiscal '26 The World Cup may be over but a reminder of the staggering sums footballers are paid has emerged from an unexpected quarter: NetApp's latest signing to its squad of execs. Chief Product Officer Syam Nair, who succeeded Harvinder Bhela in July last year after moving from Zscaler, is being made to feel very welcome, judging by the sums involved. According to NetApp's proxy statement ahead of its annual shareholder meeting in September, Nair received total compensation of $34.27 million in the fiscal year ended April 24, despite joining in July. Nair's reported compensation included $30.68 million in stock awards, derived from a $31.85 million target equity grant described by NetApp as a "make-whole" award for equity forfeited when he left Zscaler, where he was CTO. He was also promised a $5 million signing bonus, half of which was paid during fiscal 2026 and included in the total. The second half was due after his first anniversary, with repayment provisions applying if he leaves within 24 months. As The Reg has previously pointed out, it's tough at the top for both the overpaid superstars of the beautiful game and the prima donnas who professionally kick a ball around a field. Still, unlike many football teams that are losing money, at least NetApp was in the black in fiscal 2026. The American storage biz grew revenue 5.4 percent to $6.93 billion, and operating income bounced 25 percent to $1.67 billion. Like some of its peers, NetApp's share price is riding high - up roughly 60 percent in the year to date - amid surging demand for AI-ready infrastructure. More than 1,100 AI and data preparation deals were logged in the year, with 500 coming in the final quarter. That trading performance and buoyant market sentiment flowed directly into the C-suite's coffers. The star striker - sorry for the labored football analogy; let's kick that into touch - CEO George Kurian had to make do with $22.16 million. NetApp says 95 percent of his target direct compensation is "at risk," taking the form of cash incentives and equity awards rather than guaranteed salary. Kurian's base salary of $1 million hasn't moved in years, and most of the uplift came from annual incentive payouts and long-term equity awards. The compensation committee added an "individual performance modifier" in fiscal 2026 that lets it adjust each exec's incentive payout by plus or minus 15 percent based on personal contribution, layered on top of NetApp's financial results. President Cesar Cernuda received the maximum 15 percent upward adjustment to his annual incentive payout, with NetApp citing customer wins and revenue growth. His total compensation came to $11.13 million. CFO Wissam Jabre, another relative newcomer who joined from Western Digital in March 2025, received $11.49 million , lower than the $18.26 million he received the year before when he got a "make-good" bonus of $6.56 million. Exec pay doesn't seem to be a cause of ire for NetApp investors. At the 2025 annual meeting, the advisory "say-on-pay" vote passed with roughly 94 percent support. NetApp's compensation committee cited that result as validation for keeping its pay structure largely intact this year. Still, as is typical at such events, executive compensation is among the governance items on the ballot for this year's annual shareholder meeting in September, giving NetApp investors a non-binding vote on pay at the top. If only football fans had the same rights. ®

title: The Nothing Ear 3A look great… and sound good enough
teaser: The Nothing Ear 3A earbuds offer robust audio customization for just $99, despite minor flaws in ANC stability and call clarity.
summary: Reviewing the Nothing Ear 3A earbuds, the author highlights their transparent design and impressive value at $99. While the default sound is overly bass-heavy, the extensive parametric EQ (with four presets and an advanced 3-band/8-band options) allows for deep customization, significantly improving audio balance. Performance features include support for high-res LDAC codec and improved ANC, which filters out low drones effectively. However, the review notes minor performance flaws: adaptive ANC can exhibit sudden, disorienting intensity adjustments, and call quality is unreliable in noisy environments (e.g., sounding 'dark' when ambient noise increases). Despite these issues, the overall value—especially with enhanced controls via the Nothing X app—makes them highly recommended for their price point.
author: John.Higgins
content: Nothing has had a strong visual identity since the Ear 1 were released in 2021 for $99 and challenged the notion that a highly featured headset requires a high price. The Ear 3A have the same transparent look as Nothing's previous earbuds, with a clear case and stem design accented by a solid-colored body - this time adding a striking pink alongside yellow, black, and white options. And Nothing continues to improve both ANC and audio performance. But the Ear 3A also share the buggy performance that has plagued Nothing earbuds. While $99 is an attractive price for them, be ready to deal with some minor adaptive ANC and call quality issues. $99 The Good Great overall performance for the price Robust EQ The Bad Default sound is bass-heavy Some inconsistencies with adaptive ANC The Ear 3A have 12mm dynamic drivers and support the high-res LDAC codec, along with SBC and AAC. Their default sound is very heavy on the bass, and while it gives bass lines extra punch, the midrange - which includes vocals and guitars - gets covered by the excessive low end. Bassheads might enjoy it, but it's far too much for my taste, and I expect that will be the same for most people. Where I might ding some points for this on other earbuds, the Nothing 3A save themselves from that because of the robust EQ in the app. There's a simple interface with four presets and a custom 3-band EQ, a nice 8-band parametric EQ that gives you more advanced adjustments, and some additional EQ profiles from users curated by Nothing. In less than a minute I was able to adjust the EQ to something far more balanced to my ear (I added a downward slope to the bass below 115Hz, mid boost between 220-540Hz, another slight cut to the shouty frequencies between 2-3.5kHz, and some extra highs above 6.6kHz for a more open sound). It gave Chris Robinson's voice more presence on "Thorn in My Pride" and his brother Rich and Marc Ford's guitars nice crunch and bite as the song builds through the solo. And even with the cut to the low end, Johnny Colt's bass supports the band throughout. Nothing added a pink color to go along with yellow, white, and black options. ANC performance is improved over previous Nothing earbuds, with solid cancellation particularly in the lower mids and bass range, so low drones like air conditioners or plane cabin noise get filtered out very well. For $99, they also do a decent job with higher frequencies, but if you plan to use them consistently in a coffee shop you'll still hear orders being called out a bit. And if the high ANC setting is too much for you, there are mid and low settings that let in a bit more of the low end to ground you in reality. There's also an adaptive ANC setting, but here's where some of the minor issues I encountered started. While out on walks around the neighborhood, occasionally (maybe two or three times during an hour walk) the ANC intensity would quickly adjust to let in much more ambient noise and then switch back to its previous level. The whole experience lasted maybe two seconds each time and was disorienting. I tried to take note of what might have triggered it, but couldn't find a consistent situation that would cause it to happen. In general, whenever the adaptive ANC makes a change to the intensity, it's sudden instead of the more gradual change that my Apple AirPods Pro 3 or Sony WF-1000XM6 do - for hundreds of dollars more. The one issue I was able to figure out, also about volume attenuation, was with my call quality. While talking to a friend I regularly call when testing earbuds, if I was just listening to him, he couldn't hear anything from my side at all. No traffic, no wind, no breathing, nothing. At one point he wondered aloud if the call had disconnected. When I was talking, I sounded clear and natural to him if I started talking when there wasn't a lot of ambient noise around me. When the sound around me got louder - such as more cars driving by - a bit of that sound leaked through, although my voice still sounded natural. But if I started talking while there was a lot of noise around me, my voice sounded dark as the earbuds strongly filtered out upper-mid and high frequencies, including doing a great job tamping down the loud ambient sound. The Ear 3A have the same transparent design Nothing has used since the introduction of the Ear 1 in 2021. The Nothing X app includes controls for ANC intensity, a great parametric EQ, and customized controls. Both the ANC and call quality issues could be addressed with future firmware updates (my testing was with firmware 1.0.1.59), and if you use one of the static ANC settings instead of adaptive ANC, or don't plan on making calls in noisy areas, then they're a nonissue anyway. The Nothing Ear 3A also include 32MB of on-device storage, allowing them to record up to two hours of a call or take an audio snapshot (Nothing's term) of up to one minute. When you then access the app, you can transfer the recordings onto your device. When beginning a call recording, a message plays to notify everyone. I can easily see the use of recording an important call to make sure you don't miss any information (although this can also easily be done through your phone), but I have yet to find a reason for the audio snapshot. It only records up to a minute of what you're listening to, not anything around you using the earbuds' microphones, at lower fidelity. It's unique to the Nothing 3A, but also gimmicky. I'm glad the Nothing Ear 3A returned to a price under $100 after the $179 Ear 3. Nothing is at its best when it's challenging what can be done for less - and I'm more forgiving of its minor flaws. While the sound wasn't my taste out of the box, the fact you can make meaningful adjustments and tune it to your preferences makes them more versatile than most earbuds at the same price. title: IT Services in Schaumburg, IL: What Local Businesses Actually Pay, Get, and Should Ask For
teaser: Schaumburg IT costs: Businesses should budget $100-$250 per user monthly, but must track separate fees for hardware & major projects.
summary: For businesses in Schaumburg, IL, understanding managed IT costs is crucial due to the area's dense mix of corporate offices, manufacturers, and healthcare providers. Comprehensive managed IT typically costs $100-$250 per user monthly. While service agreements cover essential operations (monitoring, help desk, security), they generally exclude major capital expenditures like hardware or large migrations. Beyond standard recurring support, businesses must factor in compliance needs (HIPAA, PCI-DSS) and potentially pay for professional labor ($150-$250/hour). The article advises separating recurring support from products and project work to ensure accurate budgeting.
author: Contributor
content: Schaumburg has nearly 5,000 businesses and more than 80,000 workers, making it one of the Chicago suburbs' largest employment centers. For companies evaluating outsourced IT, industry pricing guides put comprehensive managed IT at roughly $100-$250 per user per month , with the final cost driven by security requirements, support hours, infrastructure complexity, and compliance obligations. Why IT services matter more in Schaumburg than in most suburbs? Schaumburg's concentration of corporate offices, manufacturers, professional firms, warehouses, retailers, and healthcare organizations creates unusually high dependence on business IT. An outage can affect office users, cloud applications, warehouse systems, customer transactions, remote employees, and communications at the same time. The local economy combines the Woodfield business district, industrial properties near the I-90/IL-53 corridor, and companies connected to the broader O'Hare logistics belt. Zurich North America maintains its headquarters at 1299 Zurich Way beside I-90, while Motorola Solutions, whose global headquarters occupied Schaumburg for five decades before moving to Chicago in 2016, still maintains offices in the village. That business mix creates very different technical requirements within a relatively small geographic area. A 40-person law firm may depend primarily on Microsoft 365, document management, Microsoft Entra ID, secure remote access, and reliable backup. A 100-user warehouse may also depend on industrial Wi-Fi, scanners, shipping stations, shared workstations, VPN connections, printers, switches, and line-of-business applications. Manufacturing and logistics businesses along the I-90 corridor may operate outside a standard 9-to-5 schedule, making monitoring and after-hours incident handling more important. Accounting firms may face FTC Safeguards Rule requirements, healthcare practices may need HIPAA-related controls, and organizations accepting card payments may need to account for PCI-DSS requirements. For businesses with 10-200 employees, the practical question is therefore not simply whether an IT provider can fix computers. The provider needs to support the specific mix of endpoints, identity systems, cloud applications, networks, cybersecurity controls, backups, and compliance requirements that keeps the organization operating. What managed IT services include (and what they don't)? A comprehensive managed IT agreement normally covers recurring IT operations: monitoring, help desk support, endpoint security, patching, backup monitoring, and Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace administration. It usually does not mean that hardware, software licenses, major migrations, cabling, or every technology project is included in one flat monthly fee. Industry-standard managed services usually start with 24/7 remote monitoring and management . An RMM platform such as NinjaOne can monitor workstations, servers, system health, services, and patch status while allowing technicians to manage endpoints remotely. Help desk support typically covers recurring user issues such as password problems, Microsoft 365 errors, printer connections, application troubleshooting, workstation issues, and basic network access problems. Contracts described as "unlimited help desk" should still define which users, devices, applications, and hours are covered. Endpoint security should also be defined by function rather than by a generic statement such as "antivirus included." A modern security stack may use Bitdefender GravityZone for NGAV, EDR, XDR, or MDR capabilities; Microsoft Entra ID for identity, MFA, and SSO; SonicWall for firewall security; and Microsoft Intune for mobile-device and endpoint management. Patch management normally covers supported operating systems and selected third-party applications. The provider should be able to report patch compliance rather than simply state that automated updates are enabled. Backup services require similar precision. Platforms such as N-able Cove and Veeam can protect servers, endpoints, virtual machines, and cloud workloads, but the contract should specify what is backed up, how often backups run, how long data is retained, whether immutable copies exist, and how recovery is tested . Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace administration may include account provisioning, mailbox administration, security configuration, permissions, user changes, and licensing management. The recurring service fee does not necessarily include the actual Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace license cost. A useful managed-services proposal therefore separates recurring support from products and project work. That distinction makes two competing monthly prices much easier to compare. What's usually NOT in the flat fee? Managed IT flat fees usually exclude irregular or capital-intensive costs such as hardware, third-party software licenses, major migrations, office moves, structured cabling, and large infrastructure projects. After-hours project work and emergency support may also be charged separately depending on the provider's contract. Industry pricing guides commonly place out-of-scope professional-services labor around $150-$250 per hour . A Microsoft 365 migration, server replacement, firewall redesign, office relocation, or major network upgrade may therefore be quoted as a separate project. Onboarding is another common additional cost. Industry pricing guides often place onboarding at approximately 1-2 months of recurring service , although the amount depends on documentation quality, endpoint count, security remediation, network complexity, and the amount of tooling that must be deployed. Hardware is normally separate because a managed-service fee pays for ongoing operations rather than ownership of laptops, servers, switches, access points, and firewalls. Software licenses may also appear as separate line items even when the provider manages those applications. Before signing, ask the provider to place every service into one of four categories: included in the monthly fee, separately licensed, billable project work, or excluded . That classification is more useful than a vague promise of "all-inclusive IT." How much do IT services cost in Schaumburg? A Schaumburg business should generally budget about $100-$250 per user per month for comprehensive managed IT. Industry pricing guides commonly place total monthly spending for a typical 10-50-employee company around $1,500-$5,000, with cybersecurity, compliance, multiple sites, and complex infrastructure pushing costs higher. The pricing structure matters because two providers can quote similar monthly totals while including very different services. Pricing model Typical market range Best fit Per-user $100-$250/user/month Office-heavy businesses where employees use multiple devices and Microsoft 365 Per-device About $30-$150/device/month Businesses with shared PCs, warehouse stations, servers, kiosks, or specialized endpoints Tiered Varies by service tier and security scope Companies choosing predefined basic, standard, or security-focused packages Co-managed Varies substantially by retained internal IT responsibilities Businesses with internal IT staff outsourcing selected functions These figures are budgeting benchmarks rather than standardized tariffs. Per-user pricing is easier to compare across industry pricing guides, while per-device, tiered, and co-managed pricing depends more heavily on the number of supported systems and the exact division of responsibility. A 30-user accounting firm near Woodfield may pay more per user than another 30-person business if the agreement includes advanced email security, immutable backups, Microsoft Entra ID controls, endpoint detection and response, and FTC Safeguards Rule support. A 100-user warehouse near the I-90/IL-53 corridor may create a different cost structure. Its environment may include 100 employees but 160 managed devices, shared terminals, scanners, warehouse Wi-Fi, switches, firewalls, printers, shipping systems, and multiple operational shifts. The monthly figure therefore matters less than the scope behind it. A $125-per-user contract that excludes backup, security operations, after-hours incidents, and Microsoft 365 administration may cost more in practice than a $190-per-user agreement that includes those functions. Managed IT vs hiring in-house in the Chicago suburbs For many businesses below roughly 75 employees, outsourced IT can provide broader technical coverage than hiring one internal generalist. One in-house IT employee commonly represents roughly $80,000-$120,000 per year in salary and employment overhead while still providing only one person's working hours, experience, and availability. One internal administrator may be capable of handling Microsoft 365, endpoints, basic networking, user support, and vendors. That same person is unlikely to be equally specialized in cybersecurity, backup architecture, identity management, firewall engineering, compliance, cloud infrastructure, and disaster recovery. Availability creates another difference. One employee normally provides approximately 40 working hours per week , minus vacation, sick leave, meetings, and training. A managed-services provider can distribute tickets and escalations across multiple technicians and disciplines. In-house IT becomes easier to justify as organizations grow. Around 75+ employees , daily ticket volume, application ownership, vendor coordination, internal projects, and company-specific knowledge can create enough continuous work for dedicated internal staff. That does not make managed services unnecessary. A 100- or 150-employee company may employ an IT manager while outsourcing endpoint monitoring, EDR, backup operations, after-hours coverage, help desk overflow, or infrastructure engineering. The real comparison is therefore not simply "MSP versus employee." Businesses should compare the cost and capabilities of the entire IT operating model required to support their users. Fully managed vs co-managed: which model fits your business? Fully managed IT gives an outside provider primary responsibility for day-to-day IT operations, while co-managed IT supplements an existing internal IT team. The core difference is ownership and control: fully managed service replaces the internal IT function, while co-managed service divides responsibilities between internal staff and the provider. Responsibility Fully managed Co-managed Help desk Primarily MSP Internal team, MSP, or shared Monitoring and patching Primarily MSP Often MSP Cybersecurity operations Primarily MSP or security partner Shared or selectively outsourced Business-specific applications Shared with management/application vendors Often led internally IT strategy MSP with business leadership Internal IT leadership with MSP input Escalation engineering MSP MSP supports internal IT A 35-person construction company without an IT employee may be a strong fit for fully managed service. The provider can take primary responsibility for workstations, Microsoft 365, identity, mobile devices, backup, patching, endpoint security, firewall management, and user support. A 120-person manufacturer may have different requirements. An internal IT manager may understand ERP workflows, production systems, vendor relationships, and operational priorities better than an external provider ever could. Co-managed IT allows that internal manager to retain control while outsourcing selected functions such as 24/7 monitoring, EDR, backup infrastructure, patching, help desk overflow, or complex Microsoft 365 work. The division must be documented. A written responsibility matrix should identify who owns endpoint security, user onboarding, Microsoft 365 administration, firewall changes, backup testing, vendor management, procurement, projects, and incident response. Shared responsibility without named ownership creates gaps. During a ransomware incident or major outage, "we thought the other team handled it" is not an acceptable operating model. How to choose an IT services company in Schaumburg? 7 criteria A Schaumburg business should evaluate an IT provider across 7 areas: response performance, security architecture, contract terms, engineering depth, local service capability, compliance experience, and reporting. Each area should be supported by measurable service levels, named technologies, documented processes, or verifiable technical credentials. Criterion 1 - Measure response performance A provider that advertises 24/7 support should define what 24/7 actually means. Ask for average response times, SLA targets by severity, first-contact resolution rates, escalation procedures, and whether the first responder is an engineer or an intake agent. Criterion 2 - Require a named security stack A provider should be able to identify the technologies protecting endpoints, identities, networks, and backups. Examples include Bitdefender GravityZone for NGAV/EDR/XDR/MDR, SonicWall for firewall security, Microsoft Entra ID for MFA and SSO, and Microsoft Intune for device management. Criterion 3 - Compare contracts, not monthly prices A $140-per-user proposal and a $190-per-user proposal cannot be compared without examining scope. Review contract length, termination rights, onboarding fees, after-hours charges, project rates, hardware exclusions, licensing, SLA commitments, and documentation ownership. Criterion 4 - Verify engineering depth A 100-user organization should not depend on one technician for desktops, networks, cybersecurity, Microsoft 365, backups, and cloud systems. Certifications such as Microsoft and CompTIA credentials provide one verifiable signal, while a documented escalation structure provides another. Criterion 5 - Test local service capability A provider serving the Woodfield area, I-90/IL-53 corridor, and Schaumburg industrial districts should explain where technicians are based and how on-site work is dispatched. A local telephone number does not prove that a provider has practical field coverage in the northwest suburbs. Criterion 6 - Match compliance knowledge to your industry Healthcare practices may need HIPAA-related safeguards. Businesses handling payment-card data may need PCI-DSS controls. Financial organizations and certain accounting environments may fall under the FTC Safeguards Rule, while other organizations may map security controls against NIST CSF or SOX requirements. Criterion 7 - Require measurable reporting and planning Useful reports should quantify patch compliance, backup status, endpoint-security coverage, recurring ticket categories, asset lifecycle, and SLA performance. Strategic reviews should convert those metrics into a 12-36-month plan for hardware replacement, security improvements, cloud changes, and business growth. A worked example: how one local MSP checks these boxes? RIT Company provides one worked example of applying these criteria to a provider serving Schaumburg from nearby Addison , about 15 minutes away, with typical on-site travel of 20-25 minutes. Its managed IT services in Schaumburg include NinjaOne for 24/7 RMM, Bitdefender GravityZone NGAV with EDR/XDR/MDR, SonicWall, Cytracom ControlOne, Microsoft Entra ID, NinjaOne MDM and Intune, plus NinjaOne Backup, N-able Cove immutable cloud backups, and Veeam. The company reports an average help-desk response under 15 minutes, 70-80% first-contact resolution, a 99.9% uptime SLA measured monthly, month-to-month contracts, 80+ business clients, approximately 1,000 managed endpoints, and Microsoft- and CompTIA-certified engineers with more than 100 years of combined hands-on experience. Its stated compliance support covers HIPAA, PCI-DSS, SOX, the FTC Safeguards Rule, and NIST CSF, giving a prospective buyer concrete service, security, contractual, and compliance claims to verify during due diligence. Red flags when hiring IT support in Schaumburg The biggest warning signs are undefined service scope, vague cybersecurity claims, weak contract exit terms, no measurable response data, unclear backup ownership, and dependence on a single technician. Any provider that cannot explain these areas in writing creates operational and financial risk before the contract begins. Red flag What to ask "We handle cybersecurity" without named controls Which EDR, MFA, firewall, backup, and monitoring products are deployed? "Unlimited support" without defined exclusions Which requests become separately billable projects? Long contract with difficult termination What are the termination rights after month 6 or month 12? "24/7 support" without response metrics What are the response targets for critical and normal tickets? "Backup included" without recovery targets What are the RPO, RTO, retention, immutability, and restore-testing procedures? One technician without an escalation map Who handles security, networking, Microsoft 365, backup, and after-hours escalation? Credential ownership is another important warning sign. The client organization should retain appropriate ownership or administrative control over domains, Microsoft 365 tenants, cloud subscriptions, firewall configurations, backup data, and other business-critical systems. Documentation should also be portable. A company changing providers should be able to obtain an asset inventory, network documentation, licensing information, administrative credentials, vendor records, and relevant configuration details without a prolonged dispute. Ask how offboarding works before signing the original agreement. A responsible provider should be able to describe the process for transferring credentials, documentation, licenses, and operational knowledge to another provider. Security claims deserve the same scrutiny. Statements such as "100% protected," "unhackable," or "zero risk" are not credible cybersecurity commitments because no technical control eliminates all risk. FAQ 1. How much should managed IT services cost for a small business in Schaumburg? Industry pricing guides put comprehensive managed IT at roughly $100-$250 per user per month . A typical business with 10-50 employees may spend approximately $1,500-$5,000 monthly , with higher costs for 24/7 operations, advanced cybersecurity, compliance obligations, multiple locations, or complex network infrastructure. 2. What do managed IT services include? A typical full-service agreement includes 24/7 monitoring , remote help desk support, endpoint security, patch management, backup monitoring, and Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace administration. More comprehensive agreements may also cover firewalls, EDR/XDR, Microsoft Entra ID, Intune, cloud systems, and monthly or quarterly strategic reviews. 3. What is not included in managed services? Hardware, third-party software licenses, major migrations, office moves, structured cabling, and large infrastructure projects are commonly excluded from flat fees. Industry pricing guides often place separate project work around $150-$250 per hour , while onboarding can cost approximately 1-2 months of recurring service . 4. Is managed IT better than in-house IT? For many companies below approximately 75 employees , managed IT can provide broader technical coverage than one generalist. One internal IT employee may cost roughly $80,000-$120,000 annually with salary and employment overhead , while larger organizations may gain more value from combining internal IT leadership with an external provider. 5. What is the difference between managed and co-managed IT services? Fully managed IT makes the provider primarily responsible for help desk, monitoring, security, patching, and other recurring operations. Co-managed IT supplements internal staff. A 120-employee manufacturer , for example, may retain 1 internal IT manager while outsourcing 24/7 monitoring, EDR, backups, or escalation engineering. 6. How do I choose an IT service provider in Schaumburg? Evaluate at least 7 areas : response performance, security stack, contract terms, engineering depth, local service capability, compliance experience, and reporting. Ask for written SLAs, support exclusions, backup responsibilities, escalation procedures, and termination terms rather than choosing solely on the lowest monthly per-user price. Choosing an IT provider should start with a documented scope rather than a sales presentation. Compare 2-3 providers using the same employee count, locations, security requirements, support hours, compliance needs, and project assumptions, then review exclusions and SLAs line by line. A free 15-minute discovery call, including the one offered by RIT Company, is a low-risk way to evaluate whether a provider asks the right operational questions before recommending a contract. title: Winamp aims for a comeback with a new music player powered by Deezer
teaser: Winamp is returning to the streaming era with Deezer's backing, aiming to revive a beloved classic player for modern music fans.
summary: Nostalgic classic Winamp is making a comeback through a major partnership with Deezer. Under the agreement, Deezer will power the new premium subscription service, allowing Winamp to maintain its original branding while leveraging Deezer's global licensed music catalog via 'white-label technology.' The next-generation player aims to revolutionize the streaming experience by consolidating local libraries, podcasts, and internet radio in one app. While facing a saturated market dominated by giants like Spotify, Winamp is betting on its community appeal, noting that its free desktop player is used by over 40 million users.
author: Lauren Forristal
content: Long before Spotify, Winamp was the music player of choice for millions of music fans. Now, the nostalgic brand is preparing for yet another comeback. Winamp and Deezer announced a partnership on Wednesday that will see Deezer power Winamp's upcoming premium music subscription service. Under the agreement, Winamp will leverage Deezer's white-label technology and global licensed music catalog while maintaining its own branding and user experience. The partnership is part of a larger relaunch centered around the next-generation Winamp Player, scheduled to arrive in the first half of 2027. According to the companies, the new player is designed to "reinvent the music player for the streaming era" by combining premium music streaming with users' local music libraries, internet radio stations, podcasts, personal cloud-based collections, and other audio sources within a single app. While a lot of the details remain under wraps, Winamp promises an emphasis on personalization through a customizable interface, social features, and ways to discover, organize, and enjoy music. The company asserts that its subscription service will "deliver a fundamentally different experience from today's traditional digital streaming platforms." Though loyal Winamp users who grew up during the MP3 boom are likely to be excited by this news, it's unclear whether many people will choose to pay for yet another music subscription. The streaming market is already saturated with giants like Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube Music. However, Winamp touts that its free desktop player is actively used by more than 40 million users. The announcement also reflects a resurgence of retro tech . Cassette tapes, MP3 players, and even iPods have all seen renewed interest recently as users embrace more nostalgic ways to experience music. Winamp is betting that its music player can make a comeback with modern streaming built in. While Winamp has undergone several revamps over the years, this may be its most deliberate return to its core audience. During the web3 boom, it explored NFT integration , enabling users to link music-related NFTs to their player. Previous plans included transforming Winamp into a cross-platform mobile audio app. More recently, the company has pivoted toward supporting creators, launching tools for artists , including monetization, fan engagement, and music distribution services.

content: Over the last few years, CD Projekt Red put a ton of work into fixing Cyberpunk 2077 , squashing bugs, polishing content, and even launching new DLC in 2023, Phantom Liberty . As a result, this game has gone from a source for funny, glitch-fueled videos to a world I've returned to a number of times to live out my futuristic fantasies. Plus, continued updates have given players more options for getting the most out of their time in Night City.

title: How to beat the resource curse in Norway (Summer School)
teaser: Discover how nations can avoid the economic pitfalls of resource abundance—a challenge known as the 'resource curse'.
summary: This conceptual summary outlines challenges faced by resource-rich economies, such as Norway's experience. The core issue is the 'resource curse' (or 'Dutch disease'), which describes how an overreliance on natural resource extraction can destabilize or hinder a nation’s non-commodity sectors. Key economic issues discussed include the 'paradox of plenty,' where abundant resources do not guarantee sustainable development, alongside systemic challenges like the 'coordination problem' and the 'free-rider problem.' Although it supports basic sketching features like layers and shading, an iPad Pro is a better tablet if you're serious about drawing.
